intro: Every town has places to play. Some are parks. Some are school gyms. Some are fields with tall lights. People in the town paid for them together.
Games need rules too. Some rules are painted lines. Some are printed in books. In 1863, clubs in London wrote rules for football. In 1900, Illinois high schools began the IHSA.
In this unit, you will meet real places and real rule books. You will learn who paid for them and who wrote them. You will see how they help strangers play together.
bigQuestion: Who builds the places where a town plays, and who writes the rules everyone shares?

title: Our Field

chapters.title: Park, Gym, Lights
chapters.bigQuestion: Who pays for the parks, gyms and lighted fields where a town plays?

story.title: Lights Before the Crowd
story.kicker: Friday lights click on over an empty field before anyone arrives.
paragraphs: It is Friday. The sun goes down behind a high school. The field is empty. Then tall poles click on. The grass turns bright green.
Nobody has come yet. But somebody already paid for this field. The town paid for the grass. The school district paid for the poles and the bulbs.
Soon cars will park. Families will fill the bleachers. They did not each buy a field. They share one field that the whole town paid for.
A place like this is a civic place. Civic means it belongs to the people of a town. Parks and school gyms are civic places too.
story.think: Who do you think paid for the park or gym closest to your school?

lessons.title: Lincoln Park Gets Its Name
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago turned old city land into Lincoln Park, a park for everyone.
reading: Lincoln Park sits by Lake Michigan in Chicago. Long ago, part of this land was a city cemetery. Chicago moved the graves and made a park.
In 1865, the city named it Lincoln Park. That year, President Abraham Lincoln had died. A *public park* is open to everyone in town.

words.d: land a city keeps open so everyone can use it

look.title: From Cemetery to Park
look.text: Part of Lincoln Park began as Chicago's City Cemetery. The city moved the graves and renamed the park after Abraham Lincoln in 1865.
look.cite: Chicago Park District, history of Lincoln Park

check.why: The city named the park for President Abraham Lincoln in 1865.

lessons.title: Small Parks With Field Houses
lessons.mainIdea: In 1905, Chicago opened small parks with field houses near homes.
reading: Many Chicago children lived in crowded blocks. Big parks were far away. In 1905, the South Side opened small parks close to homes.
Each park had a *field house*. It held a gym, showers and meeting rooms. Families could walk there. Later, in 1934, Chicago joined its park groups into one Chicago Park District.

a local public group that runs parks and park buildings

lessons.title: Who Pays for a School Gym
lessons.mainIdea: A public school gym is paid for with money the whole town shares.
reading: A *school district* runs the public schools in a town. People who live there pay taxes. Some of that tax money builds and fixes schools.
A school board votes on how to spend the money. A new gym needs that vote. The gym holds classes by day and games after school.

words.d: the public group that runs the schools in a town
money people pay to their town or state to pay for shared things

lessons.title: Naismith's Winter Gym
lessons.mainIdea: Basketball began in a gym in Springfield, Massachusetts, in December 1891.
reading: James Naismith taught at a YMCA school in Springfield, Massachusetts. Winter was cold. His class could not play outside.
In December 1891, he needed an indoor game. He hung two peach baskets in the *gym*. His class of eighteen men played the first basketball game.

words.d: a large indoor room for exercise and games

lessons.mainIdea: Chicago's 1893 world's fair showed how electric lights could fill a place at night.
reading: In 1893, Chicago held a giant fair. It was called the World's Columbian Exposition. Millions of people came.
At night, thousands of *electric lights* lit the fair buildings. People could stay after dark. Later, towns used electric lights on fields too.

chapters.title: A Rule You Can Say
chapters.bigQuestion: How do written rules and marks on the ground let strangers play one game?

story.title: Two Classes, One Line
story.kicker: Two children from different classes meet at a painted line and both know what it means.
paragraphs: It is recess. Two classes come out of two doors. They do not know each other. They all walk to the same white line on the blacktop.
Maya is in first grade. Leo is in second grade. They have never met before today. Both of them stop at the line. Both of them wait.
Nobody had to explain it. A grown-up painted the line long ago, before either child came. The paint says wait here to everyone who sees it.
Sports grew the same way. People wrote rules down and marked the ground. Then players from far apart could share one game.
story.think: What lines or marks are painted on your playground? What does each one tell you?

lessons.title: Flags at the Corners
lessons.mainIdea: The first Football Association rules in 1863 marked the field with flags.
reading: In 1863, a group in England wrote rules for football. We call that game soccer. Rule one was about the ground.
The ground could be up to 200 yards long. It could be up to 100 yards wide. *Flags* marked where it ended. Anyone could see the edges.

words.d: a cloth on a pole; in 1863 flags marked the edges of a football ground

look.title: Rule One, 1863
look.text: The longest the ground may be is 200 yards. The widest it may be is 100 yards. Flags mark the length and the width.
look.cite: The Football Association, Laws of the Game, 1863, Law 1
look.prompt: How did players know where the ground ended?

check.q: What marked the edges of the ground in 1863?
check.why: The 1863 rules said flags mark the length and width.

check.q: How long could the 1863 ground be?
check.why: Rule one set the longest ground at 200 yards.

check.q: In the United States we call this game
check.why: Association football is called soccer in the United States.

lessons.title: Thirteen Rules on a Wall
lessons.mainIdea: Naismith wrote thirteen short rules for basketball and posted them in the gym.
reading: James Naismith wrote thirteen *rules* for his new game. He typed them up. The rules were pinned on the gym wall.
In January 1892, the school paper printed them. It was called The Triangle. Now people far away could read the rules too.

words.d: a sentence that tells how a game is shared

lessons.title: A Meeting in a Tavern
lessons.mainIdea: On 26 October 1863, clubs met in London and began the Football Association.
reading: Long ago, English towns played football in different ways. One school allowed carrying the ball. Another did not.
On 26 October 1863, club leaders met at the Freemasons' Tavern in London. They started the *Football Association*. In December 1863, it agreed on one set of rules.

words.d: the group started in London in 1863 to write shared football rules
a group of people who play a sport together

lessons.title: A Board Keeps the Book
lessons.mainIdea: Since 1886, a board called IFAB has kept soccer's rule book.
reading: England, Scotland, Wales and Ireland each had football groups. In 1886, they formed a board to share one rule book. It is called *IFAB*.
IFAB still writes the *Laws of the Game*. Law 5 is about the referee. In 1891, the rules put the referee on the field.

words.d: the International Football Association Board, which writes soccer's rules

lessons.title: Schools Join Together
lessons.mainIdea: Since 1900, the IHSA has written rules that Illinois high schools share.
reading: In 1900, Illinois high schools formed the *IHSA*. That stands for Illinois High School Association. Schools join it by choice.
Member schools agree to its *by-laws*. The by-laws say who may play and how state contests run. A school in Rockford and one in Cairo follow the same book.
